page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Male organ vs female organ
lines: Antheridium: the male sex organ of
Archegonium: the female sex organ of the
same groups. It is flask shaped.
steps.why: The two organs are named by the gamete they make, so the male–female contrast is the whole first difference. Both are multicellular and occur in bryophytes and pteridophytes; the flask shape belongs only to the archegonium.
common_mistakes: Writing that the antheridium is the female organ. The archegonium is the female one.
Leaving out the flask shape of the archegonium — it is the one marked structural point.
steps.memory_tip: Antheridium and antherozoids share the start 'anther' — the male pair. The other organ, archegonium, holds the egg.
steps.margin_note: Two short contrast lines are enough — one for each organ.

steps.label: What each produces
lines: The antherozoids swim through water to
the archegonium; one fuses with the egg.
steps.why: What each organ produces is the second half of the difference — many motile antherozoids from the antheridium, a single non-motile egg inside the archegonium.
common_mistakes: Writing 'eggs' — one archegonium holds a single egg.
Calling the antherozoids spores. They are gametes, not spores.
steps.memory_tip: Many swimmers, one egg: the male organ releases many antherozoids; the female organ keeps one egg.
steps.margin_note: The boxed contrast line alone can earn this mark.
